name: Hassan Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time, Hassan. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and what you tell me is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a trainee on a bolting rig underground at Deepwater, a big zinc and lead mine. After each blast the new tunnel roof has to be pinned with long steel bolts so it doesn't fall on anyone, and my rig drills the holes and puts the bolts in. Each cut is a few metres of fresh roof, and I bolt it in a pattern, check the mesh, and move on. My offsider Duncan has done it for twelve years and still corrects my angles.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you end up underground?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I owned a tyre and wheel shop on the highway for sixteen years. A franchise made me a good offer, so I sold, put most of it into a rental unit and some shares, and went looking for something new. Mining paid well and I wanted to learn a skill from the ground up, literally. My wife Eszter works at a dental practice, and we've got Adam, fourteen, and Leyla, nine.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like learning again, and I like that the rules underground are clear: do it right or someone gets hurt. I use AI every day, on the bus I have it quiz me on ground support standards. What's hard is being the junior at forty-three. I was the boss for sixteen years, and now a twenty-five-year-old tells me my mesh is crooked, and he's right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the one we call AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now people can stop talking and get back to work. I'd say that the businesses that used AI well still got an edge, they just didn't get a miracle. I might post that on the business group I'm still in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's fine either way. I'd keep learning the rig, and I'd keep using AI for the small things it's good at. Honestly, I'd be a little disappointed, because I like a shake-up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going at Deepwater and get my bolting ticket signed off within the year. Keep buying shares each month and maybe look at a second rental. Keep using AI to study and to manage the rental paperwork.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Slightly bored, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you like a shake-up. Where does that come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From the tyre shop. Every time something new came along, run-flat tyres, nitrogen fill, online booking, the shops that jumped first made the money. I learned to like change because change paid me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk to about it at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Duncan. He thinks AI is a fad. We'd have a laugh about it at crib, and he'd say told you so, and I'd let him have it.

S0.say: He'd say people can stop talking and get back to work, and that businesses using AI well still gained an edge without a miracle. He might post it on his business group.
S0.think: He'd be fine either way, carrying on learning the rig, though slightly disappointed because he enjoys a shake-up.
S0.do: Keeps working and gets his bolting ticket signed off within the year, buys shares monthly, considers a second rental, and uses AI for study and rental paperwork.
S0.quote: Every time something new came along, run-flat tyres, nitrogen fill, online booking, the shops that jumped first made the money.
S0.fieldNote: Hassan learned to like change because, in his tyre shop, change paid. He carries a business owner's view into a junior role and handles the switch in status with humour. AI fizzling out feels like a missed opportunity to him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the one we call Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is what markets do, and the people who move first do well. I'd tell the young guys underground to learn the automated rigs now. I wouldn't ask the government for anything; I'd ask the company to train us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, bolting rigs are getting automated already, at least the drilling part. So my job will shrink, but somebody has to set up, run and fix those rigs. I'd like to be that person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the training coordinator in the first month for every course on the automated rigs. I'd pay for a short course in mining automation myself if they wouldn't. In the first year I'd aim to be the guy who supervises two or three automated rigs from a cab at the face, instead of driving one. I'd also buy a few shares in the companies making the rigs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit excited. This is the sort of thing I'm good at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Duncan. He's good at the job but he doesn't want to change. I'd tell him: you taught me bolting, now let me teach you the tablet. Whether he'd let me, I don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't ask the government for anything. Not even training money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Training's different, that's helping people work. I'm all for apprenticeships and courses. It's the cheques for doing nothing I don't like.

S1.say: He'd say this is what markets do and early movers do well, tell young workers to learn the automated rigs now, and ask the company, not government, for training.
S1.think: He expects bolting rigs to automate and his job to shrink, but wants to be the person who sets up, runs and fixes them.
S1.do: Asks the training coordinator for every automated-rig course in the first month, pays for a short automation course himself if needed, aims to supervise several automated rigs within a year, and buys shares in rig makers.
S1.quote: I'd tell him: you taught me bolting, now let me teach you the tablet.
S1.fieldNote: Hassan approaches this as a market opportunity and has a clear plan within the month. He draws a line between training, which he supports, and handouts, which he doesn't. His offer to teach his mentor the tablet in return was a warm moment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the one we call AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a huge change and the people who stay calm and act fast will come through it. I wouldn't say it's the end of the world. I'd tell people to look at what they own, not just what they earn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's a lot even for me. My job's gone, my rig job's gone, and Eszter's front desk job is gone. But I own a rental and shares, and if robots do the work, owning things is what matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first months I'd move more of our savings into shares in the companies making the robots and AI. I'd look at buying one or two robots myself if they were for sale, and renting them out, like I used to rent out tyre-fitting machines. I'd keep working at Deepwater until they paid me out, and I'd take the payout and invest it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Excited and scared at the same time. I'd be thinking about Adam and Leyla.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years' warning change for you, compared with none?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's enough to move money and maybe start a small rental business with machines. It's not enough to learn a new career, but I wouldn't try. In two years you don't change who you are. You change what you own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Adam and Leyla?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That Dad's got a plan and we'll be fine. That's true for us, I think. I'd also tell Adam he's going to learn how the business side works, because jobs might not be the way to make a living anymore.

S2.say: He'd say it's huge but those who stay calm and act fast will come through, and he'd urge people to look at what they own, not just what they earn.
S2.think: He privately finds it a lot even for him, with his job and his wife's job gone, but believes owning things like his rental and shares is what will matter.
S2.do: Moves more savings into robot and AI company shares, looks at buying robots to rent out as he once rented tyre-fitting machines, works until paid out and invests the payout.
S2.feel: Uneasy, excited and scared at once, thinking of his children.
S2.quote: In two years you don't change who you are. You change what you own.
S2.fieldNote: Hassan's free-market outlook gives him a clear answer even here: own the machines. He admits it shakes him, especially with his wife's job also at risk. His plan to teach his son the business side reflects a belief that jobs may stop being the route to a living.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the one we call AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is plenty for anyone willing to work at it. I'd tell people: learn, save, own something. I'd say the government should keep out of the way and fund apprenticeships, nothing more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years suits me well. I'd do two years at Deepwater learning everything I can about the automated rigs, then go out on my own. I think I'd do better than most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, get onto the automated rigs and learn how they're set up and maintained. Year two, leave the mine and start a small business servicing automated equipment for smaller quarries and contractors, using AI for quotes and scheduling. Buy a couple of machines to rent out by year three. Keep investing the rest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Busy and calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Leaving a well-paid mine job is a big risk with a mortgage. Why not wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the people who wait are the ones who compete with everyone else at the end. We've got the rental and a good cushion. I sold one business at forty-one. I can start another at forty-five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Eszter think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She thinks I'm mad, and she's usually right about me. But she also knows I don't go in blind. She'd want six months of our expenses kept in the bank, untouched, and I'd agree.

S3.say: He'd say five years is plenty for anyone willing to work, urge people to learn, save and own something, and want government only to fund apprenticeships.
S3.think: He sees five years as ideal: two years learning the automated rigs at the mine, then going out on his own and likely doing better than most.
S3.do: Learns automated rig setup and maintenance in year one, leaves the mine in year two to start a business servicing automated equipment for smaller quarries, buys machines to rent out by year three, and invests the rest.
S3.quote: I sold one business at forty-one. I can start another at forty-five.
S3.fieldNote: With five years, Hassan moves from investor to business owner again. He argues waiting is the bigger risk and points to his cushion. His wife's condition of six months kept untouched shows how the household balances his appetite for risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the one we call AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and anyone who complains later had their chance. I'd say it to my old business mates and on my group. I'd tell the young guys to buy a house before they buy a car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd do well, I think. But ten years is long, and long plans make me lazy. I'd have to push myself not to coast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take my time at Deepwater, maybe five years, and get every ticket going, including a part-time diploma in mechatronics, which is basically fixing machines that are part electrical, part mechanical, part computer. Then start the servicing business around year five with a proper plan. I'd buy a second rental and set up savings for both kids' studies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Confident, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes most for you with ten years instead of five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd study properly instead of learning on the run. Five years I'm a quick operator. Ten years, I'm the guy with the diploma that the quick operators call when things break.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone you'd worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Eszter's mother, and older people in our community who don't have savings. At the mosque we already help families who are struggling. I'd want that to be stronger by then, so it's us helping us.

S4.say: He'd call ten years a gift, say those who complain later had their chance, and tell young workers to buy a house before a car.
S4.think: He thinks he'd do well, but worries that long plans make him lazy and he'd need to push himself not to coast.
S4.do: Stays at the mine about five years collecting tickets and a part-time mechatronics diploma, starts the servicing business around year five with a proper plan, buys a second rental and saves for both children's studies.
S4.quote: Five years I'm a quick operator. Ten years, I'm the guy with the diploma that the quick operators call when things break.
S4.fieldNote: The decade gives Hassan time to study properly and build a business with a plan rather than on the run. His worry turns outwards to his wife's mother and older people at his mosque. He prefers community help over government help, consistent throughout.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because even with a plan, Eszter's job and mine go at once and the kids would feel it. What would help is clear rules so ordinary people can buy and run robots too, not just big companies, and cheap loans for small businesses to get started.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe who ends up owning the robots. Everyone asks who loses their job. I'm not scared of robots. I'm scared of a world where only five companies are allowed to own one.

headlineQuote: I'm not scared of robots. I'm scared of a world where only five companies are allowed to own one.
portrait: Hassan Varga is a 43-year-old trainee on an underground bolting rig at a zinc and lead mine, after sixteen years running his own tyre shop and selling it to a franchise. He has a wife at a dental practice, two kids, a rental unit and shares, and uses AI every day to study. He's traditional and free-market, supports training but not handouts, and leans on family and his mosque community. He stays calm through most scenarios and only uneasy with two-year AGI, answering every picture by owning machines and building a business around them.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because his and his wife's jobs would go at once and the kids would feel it.
whatWouldHelp: Clear rules that let ordinary people buy and run robots, not just big companies, and cheap loans for small businesses to get started.
